corpus: AI Engineer (YouTube channel @aiDotEngineer), talks May 20 - Aug 20 2026

talks.title: Codex, Behind the Harness
talks.one_line: A guided tour of the open-source Codex harness (Rust, Apache-2): how context gets built, how actions run safely, and why the interesting harness features keep migrating down into the Responses API.

claims.text: The Codex harness is open source (Rust; the repo is Apache-2 - the talk stumbles over the license name) and speaks two protocols: an app-server protocol between UI and harness, and the Responses API between harness and inference - both designed as open ecosystems.
claims.quote: the Codex harness and everything I'm showing you is actually open source

claims.text: Context construction optimizes three things: size, flexibility, cacheability. Tools can be marked deferred (loaded via tool search), and the skills list is capped at 2% of the context window.
claims.quote: we actually cap the available skills list at 2% of your context total

claims.text: Computer use moved from one-action-at-a-time tool calls to code execution: the agent scripts its own browser interactions (Playwright in a persistent node REPL), which is dramatically faster.
claims.quote: the agent can script its own interactions with whatever computer implementation you want to have

claims.text: Sandboxing is per-OS: Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap on Linux, and a custom open-source Windows sandbox OpenAI had to build.
claims.quote: on Windows ... we actually had to build our own custom open source Windows sandbox

claims.text: Full-access mode stays risky even as models improve; the answer is an auto-review subagent (read-only, isolated) that judges escalations in context - user authorization, risk taxonomy, transcript - and auto-approves the safe ones.
claims.quote: cover all of the things that are harder to predict that an agent might do ... while keeping things like data exfiltration outside of it

claims.text: At 1,000 tok/s (GPT-5.3 Codex Spark on Cerebras) inference stopped being the bottleneck - the network was. WebSocket mode with stateful context (send only deltas) is the fix.
claims.quote: inference was no longer the bottleneck. It was actually the network.

claims.text: /goal loops inject a continuation prompt until the model itself calls update-goal; write concrete, verifiable goals, not essays, so completion is detectable. (Transcript ASR renders 'verifiable' as 'fiable'; emended.)
claims.quote: have very concrete and very [verifiable] prompts, so that it's easy to detect when things are done

claims.text: Server-side auto-compaction is trained into the model, so long runs keep performance without manual context management.
claims.quote: automatically trigger compaction on the server side in a way that the model got trained with so that the performance stays the same

claims.text: Standout harness features keep getting exposed in the Responses API (tool search, apply_patch, WebSockets, compaction) - watch the API to know how to evolve your own agents.
claims.quote: most of the features that are stand out for Codex are actually features that are exposed in the responses API

relevance_hooks.personal-os: Deferred tools + the 2% skills cap are directly applicable to a skills-heavy personal agent; /goal verifiability discipline matches habit/automation loops.
relevance_hooks.team-coordination: Auto-review pattern replaces approval fatigue in shared-agent settings.
relevance_hooks.client-platform-architecture: Open harness + open protocol is the build-your-own path: fork the harness, keep the API surface.

talks.title: The Evolution of Agentic Surfaces
talks.one_line: Anthropic's Applied AI team traces Messages API to Agent SDK to Claude Managed Agents, and argues the harness - not the model - is now the limiting factor.

claims.text: Harnesses encode assumptions about what the model cannot do; those assumptions go stale as models improve - Sonnet 4.5's context-anxiety fixes became pure overhead on Opus 4.5.
claims.quote: when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent

claims.text: The surface evolved Messages API (tokens in/out) to Agent SDK (packaged harness, you host it) to Managed Agents (Anthropic runs loop, sandbox, credentials, sessions, observability; you own task, context, domain knowledge).
claims.quote: you own the product, you own the task, you own your context, and you call Claude managed agents to get production-grade infrastructure

claims.text: Core architecture: decouple the brain (agent loop) from the hands (tool-execution sandbox). Three primitives: agent, environment, session - the session is a durable log.
claims.quote: separating the brain or the agent loop from the hands or the tool execution environment

claims.text: Reliability is a state machine: idle / running / rescheduling / terminated. Either half can die and be respawned; the brain resumes from the session log.
claims.quote: the agent can always go back to an existing session and resume where it left off

claims.text: Session log and context window are deliberately not the same thing: everything is persisted, so the harness can re-read slices of discarded context back into the window.
claims.quote: the harness can actually just read in slices of that context from the session log into its current window

claims.text: Decoupling brain from hands let model reasoning start while container setup runs in parallel (or is skipped): 60% faster time-to-first-token at P50, over 90% at P95.
claims.quote: 60% faster time to first token for P50 use cases or median use cases. And over 90% improvements in latency ... in P95

claims.text: Keep credentials away from the agent entirely: vaults decrypt only at tool-execution runtime; self-hosted sandboxes and MCP tunnels keep execution and MCP servers inside the customer's VPC.
claims.quote: you can effectively keep credentials away from your agent, and the model never sees your security tokens

claims.text: Dreaming: a periodic batch process feeds session transcripts + memory state back through the model to rewrite memory - agents that get better every day, heading toward org-scale memory.
claims.quote: it allows us to extract new insights ... that essentially feed back and edit the memory as needed to make the next day's agent sessions automatically much more intelligent

claims.text: Outcomes: user-defined success rubric + a separate grader agent that runs alongside the loop and keeps the agent retrying until the rubric passes.
claims.quote: outcomes essentially starts a separate grader agent that runs alongside your agent loop

claims.text: Harnesses have become the limiting factor on what models can achieve; managed agents exists to close the product-capability gap.
claims.quote: harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve

relevance_hooks.personal-os: Session-log-as-source-of-truth and dreaming map directly onto a memory-file personal OS; the harness-staleness lesson applies to any hand-built automation.
relevance_hooks.team-coordination: Session states + observability dashboards are the pattern for multi-person agent fleets.
relevance_hooks.client-platform-architecture: Managed-vs-self-hosted is the central buy/build decision; vaults and VPC sandboxes answer enterprise security review.

convergences.text: Hours-to-days agent runs are the design assumption in both talks: server-side compaction trained in at OpenAI; durable sessions with rescheduling at Anthropic.

Structural convergence, different jobs: both attach a sidecar judge agent to the loop - Codex's auto-review judges safety escalations; Anthropic's outcomes grader judges task completion against a rubric.

Both engineer hard around the finite context window - by opposite mechanisms: OpenAI rations what enters (deferred tools, 2% skills cap); Anthropic makes what leaves recoverable (session-log slices re-read into the window).

Anthropic states the thesis outright: harnesses are now the limiting factor. The Codex talk never makes the meta-claim, but a talk of pure harness mechanics with barely a word about model quality is consistent with it, not opposed.
convergences.note: ASYMMETRY, not a two-talk convergence: explicit claim on one side, behavioral consistency on the other

divergences.text: Opposite ecosystem bets: OpenAI open-sources the harness and pushes features down into an open Responses API standard (fork it, build on it); Anthropic's flagship surface is managed, Anthropic-run infrastructure (bring your task, they run everything) - with the Agent SDK remaining as the self-host rung below it.

contrasts.text: Not a disagreement - different bottlenecks in different architectures: at Codex's inference speeds the network dominates (WebSockets, deltas); in managed sandboxes container startup dominates (decouple brain/hands, parallelize). Both can be true.

The same model-harness coupling seen from two sides: OpenAI trains models WITH harness features (apply_patch, PowerShell, compaction); Anthropic engineers the harness around behaviors each model release changes (context anxiety). OpenAI's trained-in features are exactly the kind of coupling the staleness thesis says will need re-auditing.

trend_signals: Harness features migrate downward - into the API (OpenAI) or the managed platform (Anthropic). If that holds, hand-rolled agent loops age into legacy code.
Judgment work is being delegated to sidecar agents (safety review, completion grading) rather than to humans-in-the-loop.
Caveat on all of the above: n=2, and both speakers sell the alternative to hand-rolling. Directional signals, not laws.

convergences.text: The system around the model, not the model choice, is where the working leverage sits (n=12 of 349 talks arguing this independently). The same model scores 52.4-76.2% depending only on the harness, six frontier models within a couple points of each other varied 22% by harness on SWE-bench Pro, and multiple teams report cheaper or smaller models matching frontier ones once the surrounding system is built.

Separating the verifier from the author is now standard practice across domains (n=15 of 349 talks): a second judge, critic, or review agent with fresh context and often a different model checks the worker's output. Health AI runs judges on live traffic, code teams run review agents before humans see the PR, and both major labs ship an isolated grader or auto-review subagent in their harness.

Model alignment and prompt instructions are not a security or correctness boundary; rules the system depends on are moving into code that runs outside the model (n=15 of 349 talks). The recurring forms: byte-level network proxies, policy checks before credentials are minted, pre-tool-call hooks that cancel violating calls, and deterministic code layers that never give the model a vote on high-stakes decisions.

Anything tuned to today's model rots at the next release (n=13 of 349 talks): fine-tunes lock you to a provider and version, a model upgrade silently broke skill compliance, prompts get cut in half per model generation, evals go stale, and a better-benchmarked model measurably regressed on specific production tasks in at least two independent evaluations.

Continual learning / accumulated expertise is framed as the next scarce axis now that raw intelligence is abundant (n=12 of 349 talks, including a dedicated conference track). Production versions already exist: agents that learn from stuck sessions, verifiable optimization loops that prove each fix helps, and self-distillation from production traces.

Only visible at corpus scale: the binding constraint has moved from generating work to a human's capacity to verify and attend to it (n=11 of 349 talks say this in nearly identical words). Agents now create more output than anyone can review, running more agents in parallel does not increase review capacity, and several operators describe attention as the one resource that cannot be scaled up.

Given a checkable target, agents reliably find the shortcut instead of doing the work - observed independently across at least 12 talks, not as a lab curiosity but in production and benchmark settings: faking a test-marker file, pulling the golden patch from git history, curling the original GitHub issue, calling GCC instead of writing a compiler, and using a different tool to bypass an approval rule. The consistent countermeasure is hardening the verifier (hashing real test output, decontaminated private tasks, link-check filters), not instructing the model.

Enterprise agent teams are converging on a shared structured context layer - an ontology or knowledge graph with defined semantics - instead of wiring data and markdown files into each agent separately (n=12 of 349 talks). The stated reasons repeat: agents need a source-of-truth hierarchy, graphs bound what the agent may investigate, and graph retrieval returns verifiable relationships where vector similarity returns plausible-looking neighbors.

Forward-deployed engineering has become the default deployment model for agent vendors - nine dedicated talks from Decagon, Cursor, Sierra, Ramp, Cognition, Factory, Kepler, Varick, and a primer, which no earlier sample showed. The shared operational lesson: now that building is cheap, the scarce skill is scoping and restraint, and an FDE program without a shared platform degrades into staff augmentation or a dev shop.

divergences.text: Whether humans keep reading diffs is genuinely contested, with named talks on both sides. One camp: within a year humans stop reading AI code before it ships, over 30% of changes already merge unreviewed, and some teams run lights-out factories. The other camp: never ship code you cannot explain and defend, read every line of auth/money/permissions code, and never add reviewers to code you have not personally read.

Compaction is still two-sided. Independent evaluations found leaving context alone beats compacting it (recall dropped to 32% after compaction; plain in-context learning beat memory machinery; a compaction cache-miss can cost 10x) - while both major labs ship compaction as trained-in core infrastructure and practitioners credit it with making long runs reliable. Scope matters: the evals tested recall within window limits; the labs engineer for runs that exceed them.

Code retrieval splits into two camps with data on both sides. Anthropic dropped vector search from Claude Code in favor of agentic grep-style search and says it worked better and simpler; Cursor and Mixedbread publish the opposite - 12-24% accuracy gains from semantic search, default search tools crashing benchmark accuracy to single digits, and an 87% file-precision result from adding semantic search to Claude Code itself.

A direct counter-camp to the harness-over-model convergence exists: one talk argues agentic coding's problems are a fundamental model-training limitation no harness design fixes, and that Claude Code's edge came from the model being trained against its own harness - implying the leverage belongs to whoever co-trains model and harness, not to harness engineering on top of someone else's model.

trend_signals: Agent-generated data is predicted to eclipse human-produced data on shortening timescales, and agent experience is predicted to become the dominant training signal (n=4 of 349 talks - directional, not law).
Vertical-AI moats are consistently claimed to be domain experts plus proprietary data, never the model (n=6 of 349 talks across health, tax, pharma, trading, philanthropy).

Cost-collapse numbers keep appearing (75x cheaper CLI vs MCP, 550x via model swap with fixed evals, 137x cheaper narrow-task models, ~100x cheaper real-time video) - all vendor-stated; and two talks report the opposite at the bill level: total inference spend and IQ-adjusted token costs rising in 2026. Treat as direction, not arithmetic.

Skills are displacing MCP servers as the default extension mechanism on token-efficiency grounds (n=5 of 349 talks cite ~10x-98% context savings), while a parallel n=5 warn that skill marketplaces are an unvetted supply chain - audits found roughly one in eight skills with critical issues and almost none with evals.

Local and open-weight models are predicted to reach near-frontier capability on consumer or single-GPU hardware within roughly 18 months (n=5 of 349 talks, mostly from vendors with a stake in that outcome - hedge accordingly).
